job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Bianca Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My days are pretty structured, because I like lists. Up at seven, a swim at the community pool, then applications and networking calls until lunch. In the afternoon I study for the first level of the CFA exam, since it's something I can control. I rent a room in a shared house in Burnaby with a roommate called Priyanka, and my parents are twenty minutes away. I did finance at UBC, graduated in the spring with a first-class standing, and interned at a wealth management firm and at a public pension fund. No offer yet, and honestly it's been a longer wait than I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected. At the pool I'd say the tools save people a few hours a week on reports. If a friend asked, I'd say I use them now and then to tidy my emails, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel okay but not relaxed. The openings around here are real, I get interviews, and my references are good. What I can't control is that firms seem to take longer to decide, and some freeze their graduate intake for a quarter. That's not AI, it's just cautious managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More of the same, really. Apply, network, study. I'd write to my pension fund supervisor, Hamish, every couple of months, so I'm still in his head. I'd book the CFA level one exam for February and keep my spending at what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried. Every week of waiting makes the next week feel heavier, and I know I'm lucky my parents would help. I'd rather not use that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, who's an electrician, keeps asking when I'll start. He says it with love, but I hear a clock. And I have a friend from UBC who's already working at a bank, and I try not to compare, which I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priyanka, who's doing a master's, and Hamish. Priyanka says take the exam and relax. Hamish says the pension fund hires in spring, so be patient. If I had to choose I'd trust Hamish, since he's actually seen how the hiring works.

I'd tell friends I use them now and then for **emails**.
think: Firms seem slow to decide, and some **freeze graduate intake** for a quarter.
I'd rather **not lean** on my parents' help.
do: Keep **applying and networking** and write to Hamish every couple of months.
Book the **CFA level one** exam for February.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than worried: each week of waiting feels heavier.

fieldNote: Her unease is the **length of the wait**, not AI.

steps.text: Write to Hamish at the pension fund every couple of months
Book the CFA level one exam for February
Keep monthly spending where it is

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real shift but a manageable one. I'd say firms should be clear with graduates about what the jobs now include. I wouldn't post much, but I'd bring it up in interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the job I'm aiming for changes before I even get it. At the pension fund I saw juniors spend weeks pulling data and formatting reports, which a tool does in minutes. I'd guess the fund would take two juniors instead of five, and the two must be good at judgment and clients. I'm decent at that, but there'd be more competition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly, which I haven't. I'd practise building a model with an AI assistant and then checking its mistakes, since that's what firms would want. I'd keep applying to pension funds and also to insurance and asset managers. I'd budget for a longer search, maybe a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My job could shrink before I start it, and that's an odd place to be. But I feel some control, because I'm adjusting before the market forces me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The data pulling, formatting, first-draft write-ups, and basic checks. All of the stuff I did as an intern. The tasks that stay are talking to the trustees, explaining risk, and signing off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to get used to the tools early, and to pick up a skill that needs people, like client reporting or risk. And not to take a rejection personally, because the intake changes every quarter.

I'd bring the subject up in **interviews**, not online.

Apply to **insurers and asset managers** too, and budget for a year's search.
feel: **Anxious** but with some control, because I'm adjusting early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to slow down and think. I'd say governments need clear plans, and companies should say what they intend to do. I'd also say it to my parents carefully, because they'd be worried more than I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel unsteady. If AGI can do the thinking work of a first-year analyst, cheaper, then no fund needs one. I'd have spent four years and a lot of study on something with a closing window. The one thing I have is a cushion, and that's not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take stock, cut non-essentials, and talk to my parents about their plans. I'd apply to jobs in areas that need people, like healthcare administration or client advice. I'd stop the CFA exam, because it'd be a waste of money, and I'd put the exam fee in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, definitely. Two years is faster than I can plan a change of career. I'd feel like I was running to catch a train that's already moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a list for the next three months. Check savings. Talk to every contact. Find out what the province offers for retraining. The thing I'd change most is that I'd stop planning for a 40-year finance career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my parents that we all adjust together. I'd say I'm worried but I'm not alone. And I'd tell my dad that I'm interested in learning what he does, because electricians won't be replaced for years.

say: I'd say governments need **clear plans** and companies should say what they intend.
I'd talk to my parents **carefully**, as they'd worry more.
think: If AGI does a first-year analyst's thinking work cheaper, **no fund needs one**.
do: Stop the **CFA exam** and put the exam fee into my savings account.
Check what the province offers for **retraining**.
feel: **Anxious**: like running for a train that is already moving.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I was running to catch a train that's already moving.
fieldNote: Her cushion gives some **breathing room**, but she says it's not a plan.
Willing to drop a **CFA** investment of time and money in the two-year world.
Looks to her father's electrician trade as a real fallback.

steps.text: Stop studying for the CFA exam and save the fee

Apply to healthcare administration and client advice jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is real warning. I'd say it's like climate planning, you can see the date. I'd try to talk to people at the fund about what they're planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can plan for the first job and the second. I'd probably get a job, because the openings exist, and I'd have two or three years of being a junior before the real shift. That feels workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the best job offer, learn the tools there, and save at least a third. I'd also use a year to take a part-time course in something with people in it, like financial planning for families. If AGI really does arrive, I'd be positioned for advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel the pressure but I'd have a plan. That makes it more like a project than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd stop everything and pivot. With five, I'd keep the finance track and add a second one. I'd probably still sit the CFA level one, because it's cheap compared with the value, but I'd skip the later levels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop assuming I can coast. I'd start measuring how much I save, how many contacts I have and how many tools I've tried. It makes me feel less helpless.

say: I'd say five years is **real warning**, like planning for a known date.
I'd ask people at the fund what they're **planning**.
think: I'd likely get a job and have **two or three years** as a junior before the shift.
do: Take the best offer, learn the tools and **save a third**.
Take a part-time course in **financial planning** for families.
feel: **Uneasy**: pressure, but with a plan, so more like a project than a threat.

steps.text: Take the best job offer and learn its tools quickly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to get it right, and that we should use it well. I'd say people shouldn't be complacent, and I'd probably volunteer with a financial literacy group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly safe, though not carefree. A full decade is a career's first act. I'd have a mortgage by then, probably, and I'd worry about that more than AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a job, finish the CFA, and build a career at a fund. I'd stay in touch with technology by trying one new tool a year. I'd save for a deposit on a flat, and I'd keep a year's cash in a safe account as a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I'd say a three out of ten on the worry scale. A decade is long enough that I'd plan around it without losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a five-year check. If the signs say it's real, I'd shift to advice or risk, which need people. If it's slower, I'd stay on my track. The point is to look up from my screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe-ish. It's not that the risk goes away, it's that I can see more of the road. But I'd be lying if I said a mortgage wouldn't make me nervous.

I'd volunteer with a **financial literacy** group.
think: A full decade is a career's **first act**, and I'd probably have a mortgage by then.
I'd worry more about a **mortgage** than AGI.

Save a **deposit** and keep a year's cash in a safe account.

steps.text: Finish all three CFA levels while working at a fund
Try one new AI tool each year at work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where I can't see a path. What would help is a clear plan from government, retraining that's real and paid, and employers who tell me honestly if they're hiring juniors or not. A bit of honesty goes a long way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm more worried than I look. I plan so much because planning is how I handle fear. If the plans stopped working I'd be lost.

headlineQuote: I plan so much because planning is how I handle fear.
portrait: Bianca is 23, a **top graduate** in finance from UBC, renting a room in Burnaby with her parents nearby.
She is measured and centrist, and handles worry by **planning** and lists.
She uses AI tools now and then and starts using them properly once a threat looks real.
Her moods stay between uneasy and **anxious**, with the 2028 world the one with no path.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she can't see a path through it.
whatWouldHelp: A clear government plan, **paid retraining**, and honest employers about junior hiring.
